complaint: A 61-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of decreased appetite and jaundice of the skin and sclerae.

events.t: A 61-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of decreased appetite and jaundice of the skin and sclerae.
Abdominal ultrasound found dilation of the left and right hepatic ducts and the upper common bile duct, with a solid occupying lesion in the upper CBD.
She had lost 6 kg in the 3 months before admission.

There was no significant internal medical diseases history or surgical history, malignant tumor history of the liver or gallbladder system, neuroendocrine tumor history, or family history of known hereditary tumor syndrome.
No psychological and social stress factors for this case were found.
The patient had not developed any clinical manifestations and no significant family history of a hereditary tumor syndrome; thus, genetic testing was not performed.
The patient had not received bile duct drainage, surgery, anticancer therapy, or any other procedures prior to admission which involved treating this condition.
Physical examination showed mild icterus of the skin and sclerae.
The abdomen was flat and soft, with no palpable mass, no tenderness, rebound tenderness, or muscle guarding.
Murphy’s sign showed a negative result.
The costovertebral angle is for kidneys I suppose.
There was no tenderness over the liver, spleen, or kidneys.
No costovertebral angle tenderness was noted.
Shifting dullness showed a negative finding.
Results for bowel sounds were normal.

Liver function tests showed a total bilirubin level of 107.8 μmol/L, a direct bilirubin level of 79.6 μmol/L, an ALT level of 104.1 IU/L, and an AST level of 80.1 IU/L; all other routine parameters showed normal results.
Tumor markers AFP, CEA, CA19-9, and CA125 all showed normal findings.
Abdominal ultrasound results showed intrahepatic biliary dilation.

Abdominal CT results showed a nodular soft-tissue density lesion measuring approximately 1.7 cm × 1.8 cm × 1.6 cm in the upper CBD, with marked enhancement on contrast-enhanced imaging and causing upstream intra- and extra-hepatic biliary dilation; no definite lymph node enlargement or distant metastasis was seen.

Abdominal MRI/MRCP findings showed the lesion in the upper CBD, appearing isointense to slightly hypointense on T1WI, isointense to slightly hyperintense on T2WI, with marked enhancement on dynamic contrast-enhanced sequences, and high signal on DWI and low signal on ADC.
MRCP showed a focal filling defect at the level of the lesion with marked dilation of the upstream biliary system, the widest diameter approximately 1.5 cm.
Overall, imaging indicated a hypervascular occupying lesion in the upper CBD causing obstructive biliary dilation.
Based on clinical history, laboratory findings, and imaging, a preoperative diagnosis of common bile duct tumor with obstructive jaundice was established.
Laparoscopic exploration was planned, followed by local excision or pancreaticoduodenectomy depending on intraoperative findings.
Intraoperatively, the tumor was found in the upper CBD.
The superior margin was below the confluence of the left and right hepatic ducts, and the inferior margin was above the pancreas; the tumor had clear borders.
No obvious hilar lymph node enlargement was seen.
An aberrant right hepatic artery (arising from the superior mesenteric artery) had a clear plane from the tumor.
Intraoperative frozen sections of the distal and proximal bile duct margins were both negative (−).
The patient ultimately underwent common bile duct resection, cholecystectomy, end-to-side Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy, and regional lymph node dissection.

The operative and subsequent plan opted to proceed with a resection of the CBD with Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy instead of pancreaticoduodenectomy, which was based on the identification during the operation that the inferior edge of the tumor was well above the pancreatic parenchyma and there was no involvement of the head of the pancreas.

This procedure eliminated the morbidity associated with pancreaticoduodenectomy yet maintained oncologically appropriate margins similar to those of surgery in association with lesions found in the upper and middle portions of the CBD today.
The Roux-en-Y limb was created at 60 cm, and the hepaticojejunostomy was created with interrupted absorbable sutures.
A closed-suction drain was inserted in the vicinity of the anastomosis.

Estimated blood loss was 100 mL, and the mean operative time was 300 min. The patient was treated postoperatively with the same enhanced recovery methods, and clear liquid was started on the 2nd postoperative day whereas liquid diet was given on day 3.
The patient recovered and was discharged 12 days postoperatively with no complications.

Postoperative histopathology showed a tumor measuring 2.0 cm × 2.0 cm × 1.5 cm in the wall of the upper CBD, with infiltrative growth interwoven with the surrounding stroma and marked fibrous stromal reaction.
Tumor cells were arranged mainly in trabecular cords and irregular nests.

Cell borders were indistinct, with scant to moderate pale or lightly eosinophilic cytoplasm; nuclei were round to oval with fine, evenly distributed chromatin, and moderate nuclear atypia was seen focally.

Immunohistochemistry showed positive results on the tumor cells for Syn, CgA, CD56, and INSM1, supporting neuroendocrine differentiation; the Ki-67 proliferation index was approximately 10%-20%, consistent with moderate proliferative activity and NET G2 classification; strong SSTR2 positivity indicated preserved somatostatin receptor expression, supporting a well-differentiated NET phenotype; CK7 negativity argued against a typical cholangiocarcinoma immune profile; retained RB1 expression further argued against poorly differentiated NEC.
Combining the morphological and immunohistochemical findings, the final diagnosis was Grade 2 (G2) neuroendocrine tumor.
At 24-month follow-up, MRI showed no evidence of tumor recurrence or metastasis.
Based on the patient’s characteristics, we have implemented a long-term, stratified follow-up strategy centered on contrast-enhanced abdominal CT/MRI, with decreasing frequency over time.
Table 1 summarizes the stratified follow-up protocol.

Each follow-up visit includes a detailed medical history and physical examination, with close attention to symptoms suggesting recurrence or metastasis such as jaundice, abdominal pain, and weight loss.
Laboratory monitoring focuses on liver function.

It should be noted that there are currently no validated tumor markers specifically for NET recurrence surveillance; therefore, imaging remains the cornerstone of follow-up, with contrast-enhanced abdominal CT or MRI as the primary modality.
Table 2 Shows the clinical timeline of the patient.
The patient was interviewed during the postoperative follow-up period and agreed to share her medical experience.
She recalled feeling extremely uneasy when she first noticed progressive jaundice of the skin and sclera, significant fatigue, and unexplained weight loss.

Prior to her diagnosis, the most anxiety-provoking period was the time leading up to surgery while waiting for a definitive diagnosis at that point; it was unclear what the nature of the bile duct obstruction was.
When the surgical team informed her that the tumor had been completely removed and that she did not need chemotherapy after surgery, she felt a tremendous sense of relief.
Two years after the surgery, she had returned to normal life, with no restrictions on her activities, and her appetite and physical strength had fully recovered.
She is willing to share her experience to help other patients with similar rare bile duct tumors.

pearls: The combination of arterial-phase hyperenhancement and normal CA19–9 is a key differentiating feature: cholangiocarcinoma is typically hypovascular on contrast imaging and is associated with CA19–9 elevation in most patients with biliary obstruction, whereas NETs retain the rich vascular network characteristic of neuroendocrine tumors at other sites ().

Therefore, SSTR-PET/CT should complement rather than replace contrast-enhanced CT/MRI, and a negative examination should not be used to exclude microscopic disease or to reduce the extent of oncologic resection.

For resectable lesions, the clinical and imaging findings described above should be sufficient to prompt NET as a differential diagnosis and to inform surgical planning, even without preoperative histological confirmation.

The subtypes should not be grouped with G1/G2 NETs for management purposes, and multidisciplinary review is warranted before and after surgery in all NEC and MiNEN cases to determine whether adjuvant systemic therapy is appropriate.

Surgical strategy for CBD NET should be guided by precise tumor location, longitudinal extent of ductal involvement, margin accessibility, and regional lymph node status rather than by a fixed operative template.
